title: MacGyver at Scale: Winning Future Air Wars of Rapid Technological Adaptation
gist: Retired Air Force Col. George Dougherty reveals findings of the previously unpublished Project Doolittle: to win wars of rapid technological adaptation, the US Air Force should redeploy a few hundred of its uniformed scientists and engineers into small forward teams paired with theater hubs. The six-component framework covers forward presence, multi-functional teams, hubs, delegated authorities, training and modifiable equipment, drawing on Ukraine and SHADOW Tech pilots.

insights.claim: In a western Pacific exercise where adversary FPV drones shot down US helicopters between island bases, a forward Air Force Research Laboratory engineer team built software-reprogrammable radio jammers with on-site circuit boards and 3D-printed housings, restoring helicopter operations within days.
insights.speaker: George M. Dougherty
entities: Science and Engineering Demand Force Team
insights.so_what: Demonstrates demand for field-deployable EW, rapid fabrication and reprogrammable electronics in Pacific contingencies.
insights.quote: Within days, the U.S. helicopters were back in action, protected by their new jamming pods.

insights.claim: In Ukraine, innovations are prototyped near the front by military teams partly made up of tech-skilled draftees, and ad-hoc US-Ukrainian teams integrated Western weapons onto ex-Soviet aircraft with 'MacGyver-like' workarounds such as tablet cockpit interfaces.
insights.speaker: George M. Dougherty
insights.so_what: Ukraine validates the battlefield-adaptation model that the US now seeks to institutionalize.
insights.locator: In Ukraine, many innovations are first prototyped

insights.claim: A Special Operations Command team working with a cooperative program office implemented a rapid approval cycle that let it invent, approve and field about 15 MQ-9 Reaper upgrades every year.
insights.speaker: George M. Dougherty
insights.so_what: Shows a viable model for fast field upgrades on fielded platforms with cooperative OEMs.

insights.claim: The US Air Force has thousands of uniformed scientists and engineers, but nearly all manage development programs at stateside centers far from the fight, which will not suffice for a prolonged adaptation contest with a fast-moving peer adversary.
insights.speaker: George M. Dougherty
insights.so_what: Signals a coming reorganization toward forward technical units, with associated equipment and training demand.
insights.locator: Unfortunately, the U.S. Air Force is not

insights.claim: The US cannot simply copy Ukraine: it fights far from home in places like the Pacific with limited civilian help, uses an all-volunteer force with more complex equipment, and Ukraine's decentralized model has produced inefficiency and scaling problems.
insights.speaker: George M. Dougherty
insights.so_what: US adaptation needs organic, deployable capability rather than reliance on nearby commercial vendors.
insights.locator: But the U.S. military cannot simply copy

insights.claim: Project Doolittle, launched quietly by the Department of the Air Force in 2022 and co-led by Dougherty and Col. Mario Serna, synthesized over twenty pilot programs into unpublished findings on implementing rapid technological adaptation at scale.
insights.speaker: George M. Dougherty
insights.so_what: An internal blueprint likely to shape Air Force force design for combat innovation.

insights.claim: Project Doolittle identified six components that independent programs converged on: forward presence and relationships, small multi-functional teams, a coordinating hub, pre-established delegated authorities, specialized training, and equipment built for field modification.
insights.speaker: George M. Dougherty
insights.so_what: A roadmap that defines where spending will flow: training, deployable labs, open-architecture systems and procurement hubs.

insights.claim: Forward adaptation teams should be five to ten self-sufficient, specially trained multi-functional personnel who can prototype in austere conditions and collaborate with reachback experts at companies and labs — a conclusion also reached by Ukrainian military intelligence innovation cells and SHADOW Tech.
insights.speaker: George M. Dougherty
insights.so_what: Small-team model creates demand for compact, ruggedized fabrication and electronics kits.

insights.claim: A higher-echelon hub should unify forward teams, propagate and standardize solutions, and engage industrial production via agile procurement offices such as AFWERX and the Defense Innovation Unit, a role Brave1 plays in Ukraine.
insights.speaker: George M. Dougherty
insights.so_what: Field-originated solutions would scale through AFWERX/DIU — a pathway for defense-tech startups to win production work.

insights.claim: Too powerful a central hub could suppress forward-team initiative, so hub and spokes need written charters separating responsibilities.
insights.speaker: George M. Dougherty
insights.so_what: Implementation risk that could slow the reform's effectiveness.
insights.locator: Some components may also be in tension

insights.claim: US-made platforms often carry restrictive tech orders, engineering change approval processes and data rights that block field modification, unlike the improvised integration onto Ukrainian MiG-29s which needed no program-office approval.
insights.speaker: George M. Dougherty
insights.so_what: Pressure on primes' data-rights and proprietary-architecture models; favors open-architecture vendors.

insights.claim: Existing policy already allows flexibility, such as the Air Force Form 1067 process granting delegated authority for temporary or test modifications, and aircraft battle damage repair teams' approval authorities provide a precedent.
insights.speaker: George M. Dougherty
insights.so_what: Reform can proceed without new legislation, enabling faster adoption.

insights.claim: Designing systems for field modification runs counter to traditional defense contractor practices favoring proprietary architectures and vendor lock, but modular open systems approaches are mandated by acquisition reform, embraced decisively by emerging defense tech firms and increasingly by primes; IP status of field modifications remains unresolved.
insights.speaker: George M. Dougherty
insights.so_what: Structural tailwind for open-architecture defense-tech entrants versus vendor-lock incumbents; watch IP guidance on field mods.
insights.quote: Fielding systems whose hardware and software can be quickly modified runs counter to traditional defense contractor practices that favor proprietary architectures and vendor-lock.

insights.claim: Only a few hundred personnel may be needed to integrate rapid adaptation teams across the Air Force's several dozen deployable wings, drawing on thousands of uniformed scientists and engineers, warrant officers, and Spark Cells already at over 100 units and bases.
insights.speaker: George M. Dougherty
insights.so_what: Low-cost reform — modest budget impact but meaningful capability gain, making adoption likely.

insights.claim: SHADOW Tech teams deploy with containerized 3D printers, microcontroller boards, antennas and CAD software, and the Air Force Spark program is producing containerized combat innovation labs.
insights.speaker: George M. Dougherty
insights.so_what: Emerging procurement niche for deployable additive manufacturing and electronics labs.
insights.locator: Equip to Enable Rapid Modification in the Field

insights.claim: Since 2025, an Air Force Research Laboratory-led Technology Maneuver Task Force has been refining implementation, and SHADOW Tech and the Air Force Institute of Technology are developing training curricula for rapid adaptation practitioners.
insights.speaker: George M. Dougherty
insights.so_what: Institutionalization is underway — signals the model is moving beyond pilots.

insights.claim: Winning future wars will depend on deployed forces evolving faster than the enemy during the conflict itself, not only on fielding better technology beforehand.
insights.speaker: George M. Dougherty
insights.so_what: Shifts value from exquisite pre-war platforms toward adaptable, reprogrammable systems and rapid production.
insights.quote: “not the strongest who survive, but the most adaptable.”
